A '''geometric stable distribution''' or '''geo-stable distribution''' is a type of [[leptokurtic]] [[probability distribution]].<ref>Geometric stable distributions were introduced in {{cite journal |last=Klebanov |first=L. B. |last2=Maniya |first2=G. M. |last3=Melamed |first3=I. A. |year=1985 |title=A problem of Zolotarev and analogs of infinitely divisible and stable distributions in a scheme for summing a random number of random variables |journal=Theory of Probability & Its Applications |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=791–794 |doi=10.1137/1129104 }}</ref> These distributions are analogues for stable distributions for the case when the number of summands is random, independent of the distribution of summands, and having geometric distribution. The geometric stable distribution may be symmetric or asymmetric. A symmetric geometric stable distribution is also referred to as a '''Linnik distribution'''.<ref>{{cite journal|author=D.O. Cahoy|title=An estimation procedure for the Linnik distribution|year=2012|journal=Statistical Papers|volume=53|issue=3|pages=617–628|doi=10.1007/s00362-011-0367-4|arxiv=1410.4093}}</ref> The [[Laplace distribution]] and [[asymmetric Laplace distribution]] are special cases of the geometric stable distribution. The [[Mittag-Leffler distribution]] is also a special case of a geometric stable distribution.<ref>{{cite journal|author=D.O. Cahoy|author2=V.V. Uhaikin|author3=W.A. Woyczyński |title=Parameter estimation for fractional Poisson processes|year=2010|journal=Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference|volume=140|issue=11|pages=3106–3120|doi=10.1016/j.jspi.2010.04.016|arxiv=1806.02774}}</ref>
 
The geometric stable distribution has applications in finance theory.<ref name=paretian/><ref name=andrews>{{cite web|title=Time Series Models With Asymmetric Laplace Innovations|author1=Trindade, A.A. |author2=Zhu, Y. |author3=Andrews, B. |pages=1–3|url=http://faculty.wcas.northwestern.edu/~mea405/laplace.pdf|date=May 18, 2009|access-date=2011-02-27}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Limit Theorems for Continuous Time Random Walks |author1=Meerschaert, M. |author2=Sceffler, H. |page=15 |url=http://www.mathematik.uni-dortmund.de/lsiv/scheffler/ctrw1.pdf |access-date=2011-02-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719101917/http://www.mathematik.uni-dortmund.de/lsiv/scheffler/ctrw1.pdf |archive-date=2011-07-19 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Geometric Stable Laws: Estimation and Applications|author=Kozubowski, T.|pages=241–253|year=1999|journal=Mathematical and Computer Modelling|volume=29|issue=10–12|doi=10.1016/S0895-7177(99)00107-7|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Characteristics==

For most geometric stable distributions, the [[probability density function]] and [[cumulative distribution function]] have no closed form. However, a geometric stable distribution can be defined by its [[characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]], which has the form:<ref name=levy>{{cite web|title=Tails of Lévy Measure of Geometric Stable Random Variables|author1=Kozubowski, T. |author2=Podgorski, K. |author3=Samorodnitsky, G. |url=https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/1813/9075/1/TR001191.pdf|pages=1–3|access-date=2011-02-27}}</ref>

: <math>
\varphi(t;\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\mu) = 
[1+\lambda^{\alpha}|t|^\alpha \omega  - i \mu t]^{-1}
</math>

where <math>\omega  = \begin{cases} 1 - i\beta\tan\left(\tfrac{\pi\alpha}{2}\right) \, \operatorname{sign}(t) & \text{if }\alpha \ne 1 \\
                  1 + i\tfrac{2}{\pi}\beta\log|t| \operatorname{sign}(t) & \text{if } \alpha = 1 \end{cases}</math>.

The parameter <math>\alpha</math>, which must be greater than 0 and less than or equal to 2, is the shape parameter or index of stability, which determines how heavy the tails are.<ref name=levy/> Lower <math>\alpha</math> corresponds to [[leptokurtic|heavier tails]].

The parameter <math>\beta</math>, which must be greater than or equal to −1 and less than or equal to 1, is the skewness parameter.<ref name=levy/>  When <math>\beta</math> is negative the distribution is skewed to the left and when <math>\beta</math> is positive the distribution is skewed to the right.  When <math>\beta</math> is zero the distribution is symmetric, and the characteristic function reduces to:<ref name=levy/>

: <math>
\varphi(t;\alpha, 0, \lambda,\mu) = 
[1+\lambda^{\alpha}|t|^\alpha - i \mu t]^{-1}
</math>.

The symmetric geometric stable distribution with <math>\mu=0</math> is also referred to as a Linnik distribution.<ref name=laplace1>{{cite book|title=The Laplace distribution and generalizations|url=https://archive.org/details/laplacedistribut00kotz|url-access=limited|author1=Kotz, S. |author2=Kozubowski, T. |author3=Podgórski, K. |pages=[https://archive.org/details/laplacedistribut00kotz/page/n213 199]–200|year=2001|publisher=Birkhäuser|isbn=978-0-8176-4166-5}}</ref>  A completely skewed geometric stable distribution, that is, with <math>\beta=1</math>, <math>\alpha<1</math>, with <math>0<\mu<1</math> is also referred to as a Mittag-Leffler distribution.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Can One See a Competition Between Subdiffusion and Lévy Flights? A Care of Geometric Stable Noise |author1=Burnecki, K. |author2=Janczura, J. |author3=Magdziarz, M. |author4=Weron, A. |page=1048 |journal=Acta Physica Polonica B |volume=39 |issue=8 |year=2008 |url=http://th-www.if.uj.edu.pl/~acta/vol39/pdf/v39p1043.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629133648/http://th-www.if.uj.edu.pl/~acta/vol39/pdf/v39p1043.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2011-06-29 |access-date=2011-02-27 }}</ref> Although <math>\beta</math> determines the skewness of the distribution, it should not be confused with the typical [[skewness|skewness coefficient]] or 3rd [[standardized moment]], which in most circumstances is undefined for a geometric stable distribution.

The parameter <math>\lambda>0</math> is referred to as the [[scale parameter]], and <math>\mu</math> is the location parameter.<ref name=levy/>

When <math>\alpha</math> = 2, <math>\beta</math> = 0 and <math>\mu</math> = 0 (i.e., a symmetric geometric stable distribution or Linnik distribution with <math>\alpha</math>=2), the distribution becomes the symmetric [[Laplace distribution]] with mean of 0,<ref name=laplace1/> which has a [[probability density function]] of:

: <math>f(x\mid 0,\lambda) = \frac{1}{2\lambda} \exp \left( -\frac{|x|} \lambda \right) \,\!</math>.

The Laplace distribution has a [[variance]] equal to <math>2\lambda^2</math>.  However, for <math>\alpha<2</math> the variance of the geometric stable distribution is infinite.

==Relationship to stable distributions==

A [[stable distribution]] has the property that if <math>X_1, X_2,\dots,X_n</math> are independent, identically distributed random variables taken from such a distribution, the sum <math>Y = a_n (X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n) + b_n</math> has the same distribution as the <math>X_i</math>'s for some <math>a_n</math> and <math>b_n</math>.

Geometric stable distributions have a similar property, but where the number of elements in the sum is a [[geometric distribution|geometrically distributed]] random variable.  If <math>X_1, X_2,\dots </math> are [[independent and identically distributed random variables]] taken from a geometric stable distribution, the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] of the sum <math>Y = a_{N_p} (X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_{N_p}) + b_{N_p}</math> approaches the distribution of the <math>X_i</math>'s for some coefficients <math>a_{N_p}</math> and <math>b_{N_p}</math> as p approaches 0, where <math>N_p</math> is a random variable independent of the <math>X_i</math>'s taken from a geometric distribution with parameter p.<ref name=andrews/> In other words:

:<math>\Pr(N_p = n) = (1 - p)^{n-1}\,p\, .</math>

The distribution is strictly geometric stable only if the sum <math>Y = a (X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_{N_p})</math> equals the distribution of the <math>X_i</math>'s for some&nbsp;''a''.<ref name=paretian>{{cite book|title=Stable Paretian Models in Finance|author1=Rachev, S.  |author2=Mittnik, S.|pages=34–36|year=2000|publisher=Wiley|isbn=978-0-471-95314-2}}</ref>

There is also a relationship between the stable distribution characteristic function and the geometric stable distribution characteristic function.  The stable distribution has a characteristic function of the form:

: <math>
\Phi(t;\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\mu) = 
\exp\left[~it\mu\!-\!|\lambda t|^\alpha\,(1\!-\!i \beta \operatorname{sign}(t) \Omega) ~\right] ,
</math>

where
:<math>\Omega = \begin{cases} \tan\tfrac{\pi\alpha}{2} & \text{if }\alpha \ne 1 ,\\
  -\tfrac{2}{\pi}\log|t| & \text{if }\alpha = 1. \end{cases}</math>

The geometric stable characteristic function can be expressed in terms of a stable characteristic function as:<ref>{{cite journal|title=Geometric Stable Laws Through Series Representations|url=http://www.math.bas.bg/serdica/1999/1999-241-256.pdf|journal=Serdica Mathematical Journal|page=243|volume=25|year=1999|access-date=2011-02-28}}</ref>

: <math>
\varphi(t;\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\mu) = 
[1 - \log(\Phi(t;\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\mu))]^{-1} .
</math>
